editorial_queries: The passage breaks off mid-honorific after "and may Allah's prayers and —," suggesting the source text is damaged or incomplete at this point; the editor may wish to restore the full formula.

The phrase "The Messenger of Allah, narrating from him and his family, counseled Ali" is grammatically unclear — it is uncertain whether the Messenger himself is the subject narrating from others, or whether a later transmitter is narrating from the Messenger and his family.
comprehension_flags: Three terms require cultural knowledge a general reader will not have: "ham" (a pre-Islamic Arabic belief in an avenging bird-spirit), "Umm Maldam" (a personification of fever addressed directly in the ruqyah), and the fa/afa wordplay in Jibril's speech, which turns on an Arabic letter-name and a cognate noun and cannot be recovered from the English alone without the Arabic script present.
The terms sawiq and al-hamim are used without explanation; modern readers unfamiliar with classical Arabic material culture and medicine are likely to stumble on both.
terminology_notes: al-fuqqa — should be standardized book-wide; this is a fermented grain drink sometimes translated as "beer" or "barley water," but the source leaves it untranslated throughout and that practice should be confirmed as consistent.

"The Master" is applied in this passage to both the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and to Imam Jafar ibn Muhammad (Abu Abd-Allah); the book should establish a consistent convention for distinguishing the two referents when this title is used.
sawiq — confirm book-wide spelling and whether it should be italicized on first use as a foreign term; al-hamim — confirm consistent hyphenation and capitalization throughout the book.

editorial_queries: The double dash "— —" following "the father of the Prophet" appears to mark one or more missing honorifics or a lacuna in the source; it has been reproduced exactly as given.

The sentence "It was also narrated from him that singing bequeaths hypocrisy and brings on poverty" appears twice in the source — once immediately after the opening verse citation and once after the dialogue about singing — with identical wording and no discernible rhetorical purpose for the repetition; it reads as a transcription duplicate, and one instance has been retained.

The pronoun "He" opening the paragraph on withdrawal lacks a clear stated antecedent in the source — it follows the passage on the Prophet and the Imams, yet the ruling appears to derive from Ali; the source's ambiguity is preserved here as given.

The sentence "It is narrated from Ali that he said, concerning a man who married a woman in return for a young servant: neither falling short nor going to excess" appears to be an incomplete ruling — the principle "neither falling short nor going to excess" is stated without a clear grammatical subject or governing clause, suggesting the source text may be garbled or abridged at this point.
The honorific "(ع and his family)" is an unusual abbreviated form — it may be a book-specific convention or a scan/transcription artifact, and its exact expansion is unclear from context.

The passage states that "the testimony of a single upright woman is accepted in matters of breastfeeding" but immediately adds that where no upright woman is available her testimony alone does not suffice — the second clause may refer to the non-upright woman's testimony, but the referent of "her" is ambiguous and has been left as in the source.
comprehension_flags: The phrase "no woman like the daughter of one's age" — meaning a woman of comparable age or generation to the suitor — is an archaic idiom that may be opaque to modern readers and may benefit from an editorial footnote in the published edition.

"Those his right hand possesses" is a classical Quranic legal phrase referring to enslaved persons; a modern general reader may not immediately recognize it as a legal category in the same class as wives and blood relations.

Several Arabic technical terms — iddah, khutbah (in the marriage-proposal sense), walimah, khurs, idhar, wakirah, aqiqah, al-hays — appear without gloss and may be unfamiliar to general readers; a glossary or footnote pass is advisable.
The term "al-zafn" is left untranslated in the source and may be unfamiliar to general readers; it appears to denote a form of dancing or movement.

The notation "(ع and his family)" appears twice as an apparent transcript shorthand for the full blessing formula written out elsewhere in the passage; a modern reader may be confused by the inconsistency, and standardization is advisable.

The term "milk of the stallion" (laban al-fahl) is a technical legal concept unfamiliar to most modern readers; a glossary note at chapter level would assist comprehension without interrupting the prose.
terminology_notes: Nasibiyyah / Nasib — confirm that these two forms (feminine and masculine) are the book's established spellings, to be applied consistently throughout.

"people of truce" — verify whether this is the book's preferred rendering of the underlying Arabic term, or whether "people of covenant" or another phrase has been established elsewhere in the edition.
"khutbah" here means a marriage proposal, not a sermon; the book should settle on a consistent English gloss or note to distinguish the two uses wherever both occur.
hadd — confirm book-wide spelling (hadd vs. ḥadd) for consistency.
awrah — confirm this is the book's established spelling before going to press, as some editions use 'awra or 'awrah.
"Abu Abdullah" / "Abu Abd-Allah" — the source uses both spellings for what appears to be the same honorific title; a single book-wide spelling should be established.
marriage of pleasure — confirm this is the book's established rendering of *mut'ah* before standardizing.
"umm-walad" — confirm book-wide rendering (hyphenated, unhyphenated, or italicized) for consistency.
mukatabah — should be standardized book-wide; verify whether the book uses this form or "mükatabah" / "al-mukatabah" consistently.
mudabbarah — should be standardized book-wide alongside mukatabah.
hadd — should be standardized book-wide; verify whether the book italicizes it.
The honorific rendered as "((ع) and his family)" on first occurrence and "and his family" on subsequent ones — the book-wide convention for this honorific should be confirmed and applied uniformly.

editorial_queries: The sentence "Both forms of divorce are, despite the difference in wording, one in substance" follows the list of invalid divorces but is not entirely clear which two forms are being compared — the divorce of innovation and the Sunnah divorce, or two labels for the same invalid divorce; the source wording has been preserved unchanged.

In the dialogue, a man asks Abu Jafar but the response is attributed to Ali — it is unclear whether Ali is another name for Abu Jafar, a narration within a narration, or an editorial error; the tag has been preserved exactly as given.
comprehension_flags: The phrase "after four, and in al-Rahbah" may puzzle modern readers who lack context about the limit of four wives and the location al-Rahbah, but no explanatory addition is authorized here.

The terms "mudabbar" (a slave whose manumission takes effect upon the master's death) and "mukatab" (a slave who has contracted to purchase his own freedom in installments) are technical legal categories that general readers will not recognize; a glossary entry or footnote may be warranted.

The clause "she may go out in the final part of the night, provided she returns before evening" may puzzle modern readers — it appears to mean she may leave before dawn and must be back before the following evening, but the phrasing could be read as internally contradictory; a glossing note may be warranted at a later editorial pass.
terminology_notes: *iddah* — confirm book-wide spelling and italicization convention for this term.
al-Ila — should be standardized book-wide as "al-Ila" (with capital I, hyphenated prefix) to match this passage's usage.
"sa" and "mudd" — these units of dry measure appear without definition; confirm the book uses these spellings consistently and consider whether a glossary note is needed.
